Treat absent, blank, or unusable information as unknown; a truncated field supplies only its visible content. Missing information alone is neither agreement nor disagreement.

Compare book titles and contributor names after harmless normalization of case, spacing, punctuation, HTML entities, name order, and clearly recoverable encoding damage. Reconcile initials, expanded names, accents, and duplicated text only when the surrounding attributes support the same identity. Preserve meaningful words, technical symbols, version numbers, and scope qualifiers. Text in a description may use a different language from the book; do not infer a translated edition or an alias merely from that language or from broad semantic similarity.

Assess whether an identifier is usable before treating it as identity evidence. Ignore ISBN separators and compare legitimate ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 equivalents, accounting for their different check digits; do not just strip a prefix or compare a digit substring. Blank, truncated, invalid, or obviously placeholder ISBN-shaped values provide no identifier agreement. A retailer identifier in an ISBN field is not automatically an ISBN. Equivalent usable identifiers strongly support compatible book records despite weak catalog discrepancies; different identifiers can denote reprints or formats of the same work and are not sufficient alone to establish different content.

Compare contributors by role and by the whole record. Author lists can be reordered, duplicated, abbreviated, incomplete, or mixed with editors, translators, foreword writers, organizations, and title fragments. A compatible subset of contributors is not a conflict. Distinct primary creators attached to a generic title are strong evidence of different books, but a conflicting author field should be reconsidered when an equivalent usable identifier and distinctive title support a catalog error. Without such corroboration, do not invent coauthorship, a pseudonym, or an alternative identity to explain unrelated names.

Compare the distinctive title together with its author and substantive qualifiers. A subtitle, series designation, contributor credit, or descriptive phrase may be omitted, shortened, rearranged, or moved into another field. Allow this when the retained identity and available corroboration align. A common title phrase or generic subject heading alone does not establish identity, and a shared author does not merge different works. Do not discard words that distinguish the actual subject, instructional approach, content selection, or version merely to increase title similarity.

Keep different installments, volumes, parts, covered periods, and conference events distinct, even when their authors and series titles agree. Read numbering in context: an audiobook part, a book volume, an omnibus number, a subseries position, and a conference sequence number refer to different things. An apparent number mismatch is not decisive when the records use different numbering schemes and a usable equivalent identifier or explicit contents establish the same object. A missing number is unknown, not evidence that a record covers every volume; do not invent the contents of a shortened listing.

For technical and instructional books, preserve the target product or platform, software or device release, programming language, examination, instructional level, and substantive edition. Explicit incompatible versions or scopes generally indicate different books even when the author and most of the title agree. Distinguish a publication date from a release named in the title. Normalize ordinal edition wording and inspect what an edition field actually means: a calendar year or a binding code is not necessarily an ordinal edition. A missing version, or a compatible subset of a stated version range, is not an explicit conflict; seek corroboration rather than assuming equivalence or a hidden revision.

Compare the content of the object being offered. A boxed set, anthology, combined volume, materially expanded selection, adaptation, abridgment, companion manual, or separately specified supplement is not interchangeable with a constituent work or a different selection merely because titles overlap. Check descriptions and scope qualifiers as well as titles. A shortened listing can still describe the same complete object when identifiers or explicit contents support that reading. One-sided mention of illustrations, notes, media, or extras does not by itself prove a different object; retain uncertainty when the other listing's contents are unspecified.

Use publication year, publisher, pagination, price, physical dimensions, and retailer format offers as secondary evidence. Strongly aligned title, authorship, and scope can establish the same work across reprints and catalog discrepancies; a change in these secondary fields alone should not force a non-match. Publisher spellings or imprint-level differences need not conflict, but do not assume undocumented corporate relationships. Dimension order, units, and rounding must be interpreted before comparison, and dimension or page-count differences do not establish changed content on their own. A list of prices for several formats is not a definitive statement of the record's format.

Resolve evidence conflicts by specificity and reliability. Explicit incompatible work, content selection, volume, or substantive technical version outweighs generic title, author, publisher, or series overlap. A usable equivalent identifier can resolve an omitted title component or weak metadata discrepancy, but should not silently erase an explicit incompatible content claim; first look for a visible extraction error or different numbering convention. When title and author align but identifiers differ, distinguish an explicitly described content revision from an ordinary reprint. If the records cannot settle that distinction, base the decision on the supported identity evidence without inventing facts, entity-specific exceptions, or a presumption from label frequencies.
